{{Distinguish|Higman's theorem (disambiguation){{!}}Higman's theorem}}

In [[mathematics]], '''Higman's lemma''' states that the set <math>\Sigma^*</math> of finite [[sequence]]s over a finite alphabet <math>\Sigma</math>, as [[partially ordered]] by the [[subsequence]] relation, is a [[well-quasi-order|well partial order]]. That is, if <math>w_1, w_2, \ldots\in \Sigma^*</math> is an infinite sequence of words over a finite alphabet <math>\Sigma</math>, then there exist indices <math>i < j</math> such that <math>w_i</math> can be obtained from <math>w_j</math> by deleting some (possibly none) symbols. More generally the set of sequences is well-quasi-ordered even when <math>\Sigma</math> is not necessarily finite, but is itself well-quasi-ordered, and the subsequence ordering is generalized into an "embedding" quasi-order that allows the replacement of symbols by earlier symbols in the well-quasi-ordering of <math>\Sigma</math>. This is a special case of the later [[Kruskal's tree theorem]]. It is named after [[Graham Higman]], who published it in 1952.

==Proof==

The following proof, due to [[Crispin Nash-Williams]]<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Nash-Williams |first1=C. St. J. A. |title=On well-quasi-ordering finite trees |journal=Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society |date=1963 |volume=59 |issue=4 |doi=10.1017/S0305004100003844}}</ref>, uses an elegant "minimal bad sequence" argument.

Let <math>\Sigma</math> be a well-quasi-ordered alphabet of symbols (in particular, <math>\Sigma</math> could be finite and ordered by the identity relation). Suppose [[proof by contradiction|for a contradiction]] that there exist infinite ''bad'' sequences, i.e. infinite sequences of words <math>w_1, w_2, w_3, \ldots\in \Sigma^*</math> such that no <math>w_i</math> embeds into a later <math>w_j</math>. Then there exists an infinite bad sequence of words <math>W=(w_1, w_2, w_3, \ldots)</math> that is minimal in the following sense: <math>w_1</math> is a word of minimum length from among all words that start infinite bad sequences; <math>w_2</math> is a word of minimum length from among all infinite bad sequences that start with <math>w_1</math>; <math>w_3</math> is a word of minimum length from among all infinite bad sequences that start with <math>w_1,w_2</math>; and so on. In general, <math>w_i</math> is a word of minimum length from among all infinite bad sequences that start with <math>w_1,\ldots,w_{i-1}</math>.

Since no <math>w_i</math> can be the [[empty word]], we can write <math>w_i = a_i z_i</math> for <math>a_i\in\Sigma</math> and <math>z_i\in\Sigma^*</math>. Since <math>\Sigma</math> is well-quasi-ordered, the sequence of leading symbols <math>a_1, a_2, a_3, \ldots</math> must contain an [[Well-quasi-ordering|infinite increasing sequence]] <math>a_{i_1} \le a_{i_2} \le a_{i_3} \le \cdots</math> with <math>i_1<i_2<i_3<\cdots</math>.

Now consider the sequence of words <math display="block">w_1, \ldots, w_{{i_1}-1}, z_{i_1}, z_{i_2}, z_{i_3}, \ldots.</math>
Because <math>z_{i_1}</math> is shorter than <math>w_{i_1} = a_{i_1} z_{i_1}</math>,
this sequence is "more minimal" than <math>W</math>, and so it must contain a word <math>u</math> that embeds into a later word <math>v</math>. But <math>u</math> and <math>v</math> cannot both be <math>w_j</math>'s, because then the original sequence <math>W</math> would not be bad. Similarly, it cannot be that <math>u</math> is a <math>w_j</math> and <math>v</math> is a <math>z_{i_k}</math>, because then <math>w_j</math> would also embed into <math>w_{i_k}=a_{i_k}z_{i_k}</math>. And similarly, it cannot be that <math>u=z_{i_j}</math> and <math>v=z_{i_k}</math>, <math>j<k</math>, because then <math>w_{i_j}=a_{i_j}z_{i_j}</math> would embed into <math>w_{i_k}=a_{i_k}z_{i_k}</math>. In every case we arrive at a contradiction.

==Ordinal type==

The [[Well-quasi-ordering|ordinal type]] of <math>\Sigma^*</math> is related to the ordinal type of <math>\Sigma</math> as follows:<ref name="dejongh_parikh">{{cite journal |last1=de Jongh |first1=Dick H. G. |author-link=Dick de Jongh |last2=Parikh |first2=Rohit |author-link2=Rohit Parikh |title=Well-partial orderings and hierarchies |journal=Indagationes Mathematicae (Proceedings) |date=1977 |volume=80 |issue=3 |pages=195–207 |doi=10.1016/1385-7258(77)90067-1|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="schmidt">{{cite thesis |last=Schmidt |first=Diana |type=Habilitationsschrift |date=1979 |title=Well-partial orderings and their maximal order types |publisher=Heidelberg}} Republished in: {{cite book |last=Schmidt |first=Diana |date=2020 |chapter=Well-partial orderings and their maximal order types |title=Well-Quasi Orders in Computation, Logic, Language and Reasoning |publisher=Springer |pages=351–391 |editor-last1=Schuster |editor-first1=Peter M. |editor-last2=Seisenberger |editor-first2=Monika |editor-last3=Weiermann |editor-first3=Andreas |series=Trends in Logic |volume=53 |doi=10.1007/978-3-030-30229-0_13|isbn=978-3-030-30228-3 }}</ref> <math display="block">o(\Sigma^*)=\begin{cases}\omega^{\omega^{o(\Sigma)-1}},&o(\Sigma) \text{ finite};\\ \omega^{\omega^{o(\Sigma)+1}},&o(\Sigma)=\varepsilon_\alpha+n \text{ for some }\alpha\text{ and some finite }n;\\ \omega^{\omega^{o(\Sigma)}},&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}</math>

==Reverse-mathematical calibration==
Higman's lemma has been [[Reverse mathematics|reverse mathematically]] calibrated (in terms of subsystems of [[second-order arithmetic]]) as equivalent to <math>ACA_0</math> over the base theory <math>RCA_0</math>.<ref>J. van der Meeren, M. Rathjen, A. Weiermann, [https://arxiv.org/abs/1411.4481v2 An order-theoretic characterization of the Howard-Bachmann-hierarchy] (2015, p.41). Accessed 03 November 2022.</ref>
